title: mRNA Structure Regulates Translation at Every Step.
abstract: Precise, context-sensitive control of protein synthesis is critical in eukaryotic cells, and mRNA structure has emerged as a central mechanism for achieving this control. mRNA structures influence every stage of translation. During initiation, structures within 5' untranslated regions modulate ribosome association with mRNA and the balance between translation of the main open reading frame and use of upstream or alternative start sites. During elongation, structures in the coding sequence govern ribosome pausing in ways that can either protect mRNA stability or trigger decay. During termination, structures downstream of primary stop codons promote readthrough to generate protein isoforms in a tissue-specific manner. mRNA structures are remodeled by helicase expression, post-transcriptional modifications, and translational programming to provide additional layers of regulation. We review recent advances illuminating diverse mechanisms by which RNA structure modulates translation.

title: RBM4 Stabilizes S100A10 mRNA to Remodel the Tumor Immune Microenvironment and Promote Immune Evasion in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: RNA-binding protein RBM4 regulates post-transcriptional programs, but its role in shaping the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is unclear. We hypothesized that RBM4 enhances S100A10 mRNA stability to drive immune evasion. RBM4-S100A10 coupling was interrogated by expression profiling, RIP-qPCR, actinomycin D chase, and 3'UTR reporter assays. Gain/loss models (OE-RBM4, shS100A10) were used to assess migration/invasion and apoptosis. Immune consequences were evaluated by CD8+ T-cell co-culture (ELISA for Granzyme B, IFN-γ, TNF-α; IL-10, TGF-β) and immunofluorescence. Western blots probed cPLA2/5-LOX signaling. Subcutaneous/orthotopic models measured tumor growth, CD8+ infiltration, and effector subsets; S100A10 silencing and PD-1 blockade served as interventions. RBM4 positively correlated with S100A10 and bound the S100A10 3'UTR, increasing mRNA stability and 3'UTR-dependent reporter activity. RBM4 overexpression promoted migration/invasion and reduced apoptosis, whereas S100A10 knockdown reversed these phenotypes. In the TIME context, RBM4 reduced CD8+ T-cell effector function (lower Granzyme B/IFN-γ/TNF-α) while elevating IL-10/TGF-β, accompanied by diminished CD8+ infiltration and fewer CD8+GZMB+/CD8+TNF-α+ cells in vivo. Mechanistically, RBM4 activated the cPLA2/5-LOX axis (increased phospho-forms with stable totals). S100A10 silencing or PD-1 blockade mitigated immune suppression and restrained tumor growth, indicating pathway specificity and therapeutic tractability. RBM4 enhances S100A10 mRNA stability, remodels the HCC TIME, suppresses CD8+ T-cell effector function, and promotes immune evasion; targeting the RBM4-S100A10 axis may improve responses to PD-1 immunotherapy.

title: Distilling Direct Effects via Conditional Differential Gene Expression Analysis.
abstract: Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis is foundational for interpreting RNA sequencing data, but it conflates direct biological effects with correlations propagated through gene co-expression. Across three RNA sequencing datasets (including a genome-scale perturb-seq experiment), we find that only a small fraction of differentially expressed genes have direct effects on the trait of interest, while the majority are undirected or passengers whose associations are mediated through other genes. To distinguish direct effect genes, we introduce conditional differential gene expression (CDGE) analysis, a framework that tests for conditional rather than marginal association between each gene and the trait of interest. Implemented via the GhostKnockoff procedure with lasso regression, CDGE delivers false discovery rate control, operates on summary statistics from existing DGE pipelines, and accommodates batch effects. The genes identified by CDGE mediate the effects of most other differentially expressed genes and show stronger enrichment for known protein-protein interactions and biological pathways than DGE-identified genes. These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development. To facilitate public access to knockoff-based CDGE analysis, we have developed the R package "KnockoffCDGE" as an integrated implementation, which is freely available at https://github.com/GuJQ5/KnockoffCDGE (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241517). Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Mediator-associated proteins and the small RNA-guided Polycomb repressive complex enhance cryptic transcription for transposon exclusion.
abstract: Suppression of transposable elements (TEs) is critical for maintaining genome integrity. The evolutionary arms race between TEs and their eukaryotic host organisms has driven the development of small RNA-dependent mechanisms that specifically suppress TEs while leaving non-TE regions unperturbed. In the binucleated ciliate Tetrahymena, small RNAs (sRNAs) are generated from both TE and non-TE regions of the germline genome, whereas noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) from the TE-free somatic genome target and eliminate non-TE sRNAs, thereby selectively preserving TE-specific sRNAs for guiding TE recognition. Since sRNAs are produced from both strands, the counteracting ncRNAs must also occur bidirectionally. However, the mechanism by which the somatic genome generates ncRNAs from both strands remains unresolved. Here, we show that these ncRNAs arise from widespread cryptic transcription initiated outside canonical promoters and dependent on the developmentally specific Mediator complex-associated proteins Dima1 and Emit2. We further demonstrate that sRNA-guided recruitment of the Tetrahymena Polycomb repressive complex 2 and Dima1 occupancy are mutually reinforcing, promoting local accumulation of RNA polymerase II, which may facilitate cryptic transcription from these loci in a histone methyltransferase-independent manner. Disruption of Dima1 abolishes cryptic transcription, leads to aberrant accumulation of non-TE sRNAs, and results in erroneous genome elimination and cell death. These findings reveal a regulatory circuit involving sRNAs, Polycomb, and the Mediator-associated protein Dima1 that promotes cryptic transcription, thereby ensuring accurate TE exclusion and genome integrity.

title: A tunable immune-evasion function of Zika virus NS5 governs viral fitness and pathogenesis.
abstract: Type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a central antiviral defense, with STAT2 driving the expression of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) to restrict viral infection. Zika virus (ZIKV) and dengue virus evade this pathway through nonstructural protein 5 (NS5)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of STAT2, yet the contribution of this immune-evasion strategy to viral fitness and pathogenesis remains incompletely defined. Here, using a multistep mutational scanning strategy that jointly assessed STAT2 degradation and viral RNA replication, we identified a single NS5 residue, L162, as uniquely permissive to substitution that abolishes STAT2 degradation without compromising intrinsic replication functions. Substitution of L162 with alanine or glycine (L162A or L162G) selectively disrupted NS5 recruitment of the ZSWIM8-CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase, thereby preserving STAT2 stability and restoring IFN signaling. Recombinant ZIKV carrying these mutations exhibited reduced replication and enhanced ISG induction in human cells, defects fully rescued by STAT2 knockout. In A129 mice (type I IFN receptor deficient), mutant and WT viruses replicated comparably, but in human STAT2 knock-in mice, ZIKV-NS5L162G exhibited markedly reduced viral loads and disease. In pregnant human STAT2 knock-in mice, the mutant also reduced placental and fetal viral burdens and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Notably, infection with ZIKV-NS5L162G elicited robust neutralizing antibody and T cell responses that conferred protection against WT challenge. Together, these findings establish NS5-mediated STAT2 degradation as a central determinant of ZIKV immune-evasion, viral fitness, and pathogenesis and highlight disruption of NS5-STAT2 antagonism as a promising strategy for antiviral intervention and rational attenuation.

title: RSPO2 synergizes with BMP2 to enhance Wnt-dependent bone healing.
abstract: Bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP2) is used clinically to promote bone regeneration, but dose-limiting side effects restrict its clinical utility. Canonical Wnt signaling is essential for bone formation, and R-spondin-2 (RSPO2) is a secreted Wnt agonist highly expressed by osteoprogenitors. We found that BMP2 strongly induced RSPO2 during early human mesenchymal stem cell (hMSC) osteoblast differentiation. Recombinant RSPO2 synergized with BMP2 in both hMSCs and MC3T3-E1 preosteoblasts, whereas RSPO2 silencing impaired BMP2-driven osteogenic responses. In a murine critical-size calvarial defect model, co-delivery of RSPO2 and a suboptimal dose of BMP2 yielded significantly more new bone than BMP2 alone, while RSPO2 alone was ineffective. Enhanced canonical Wnt activation with BMP2-RSPO2 co-treatment was shown with an in vivo Wnt reporter mouse. Bulk RNA sequencing of MC3T3-E1 cells revealed that BMP2-RSPO2 co-treatment differentially activated osteogenesis-related genes and pathways compared to BMP2 alone. The guanine exchange factor (GEF), Prex1, was selectively upregulated by BMP2-RSPO2 co-treatment, and was required for RSPO2-mediated enhancement of BMP2-induced osteoblastogenesis. These findings identify RSPO2 as an enhancer of BMP2-driven osteogenesis, amplifying Wnt activation and involving PREX1-dependent signaling. RSPO2 or PREX1 activation may represent a co-therapy that could enhance BMP2 efficacy while mitigating the adverse effects of high-dose BMP2.

title: Substrate Selectivity of Viperin Probed Using Anticancer-Related Pyrimidine Nucleotide Analogs.
abstract: Many antiviral and anticancer drugs are based on the structure of pyrimidine nucleosides. Once phosphorylated, they function by interfering with either DNA or RNA replication or transcription. The antiviral enzyme, viperin, catalyzes the dehydration of CTP to produce 3'-deoxy-3',4'-didehydroCTP (ddhCTP), which functions as a natural antiviral nucleotide. Various drugs mimic the structure of CTP, and furthermore, viperin is upregulated in some cancers and autoimmune diseases. Therefore, we examined whether such drugs may be substrates for viperin. A panel of eight commercially available nucleosides, including several clinically used drugs, were enzymatically converted to their triphosphate forms and investigated as substrates for viperin. Five of the nucleotides were not substrates, indicating that viperin has generally high specificity for CTP. Two nucleotides, 3'-deoxy-3'-fluoroCTP and cytarabine triphosphate elicited reductive cleavage of SAM and were converted to their dehydrated products by viperin. The last compound, gemcitabine triphosphate, elicited reductive cleavage of SAM, but no dehydrated product was observed, implying that it activates SAM cleavage without undergoing hydrogen atom abstraction. The implications of these results are discussed.

title: DENV-NS1 drives novel microRNAs to disrupt cerebral endothelial barrier functions.
abstract: Dengue virus non-structural protein 1 (DENV-NS1) plays a key role in the vascular leakage associated with severe dengue; however, the molecular mechanisms by which NS1 induces endothelial dysfunction remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify a new aspect of the pathogenic strategy: the post-transcriptional reprogramming of host endothelial cells via microRNAs (miRNAs) in NS1-induced DENV pathogenesis. Small RNA sequencing and subsequent bioinformatic analysis identified novel miRNA-gene regulatory networks responsive to DENV-NS1 in human brain microvascular endothelial cells. Multiple dysregulated novel miRNAs were identified as potential regulators of critical antiviral components (STAT1, SOCS1-6, OAS1), suggesting suppressed interferon signaling. Downregulation of identified novel miRNAs targeting IL-6, IL-10, IL-1α, IL-17A, CXCR4, and CXCR5 indicates increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production and chemokine-driven immune cell recruitment, thereby worsening endothelial inflammation and vascular leakage. The simultaneous targeting of cytoskeletal regulators (RAC1, ROCK1/2) and tight junction proteins (CLDN1, CLDN2, CLDN16, CLDN22) suggests a two-phase disruption of endothelial stability, characterized by cytoskeletal remodeling and compromised tight junction integrity as a bystander effect of DENV-NS1. The downregulation of several miRNAs targeting XIAP, MDM2/4, and SMAD family genes established the involvement of novel miRNAs in apoptosis regulation and TGF-β/SMAD-mediated endothelial cell signaling. Our findings suggest that DENV-NS1 alters endothelial miRNA networks, leading to reduced antiviral immunity, increased inflammation, and compromised vascular integrity. This study identifies novel miRNA-mediated regulatory nodes that could function as therapeutic targets to prevent or mitigate dengue-associated vascular leakage.

title: Label-free fluorescent detection of miRNA-21 via EXPAR-triggered rolling circle amplification coupled with a dimeric/tandem G-quadruplex-thioflavin T reporter.
abstract: MicroRNA-21 is a well recognized oncogenic microRNA and is involved in the initiation and development of many cancers, making it an important candidate marker for diagnosis. In this work, a label-free fluorescent assay was designed for highly sensitive miRNA-21 detection by coupling exponential amplification reaction (EXPAR), rolling circle amplification (RCA), and dimeric G-quadruplex/thioflavin T (ThT) signal reporting. The designed asymmetric hairpin probe specifically recognizes the target and initiates the EXPAR, generating abundant trigger strands that subsequently activate RCA. The RCA products contain repeated G-rich segments encoding tandem/dimeric G4-forming motifs, which form multiple G-quadruplex units in the presence of K+. After ThT binds to these structures, a clear fluorescence output is generated. Benefiting from the effectively suppressed background leakage by the hairpin design and the significantly enhanced signal generation enabled by the EXPAR-RCA cascade, the assay exhibits excellent analytical performance. The fluorescence response shows a good linear correlation over the range of 10 fM to 10 nM, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.58 fM. The method also demonstrates high selectivity toward miRNA-21, capable of discriminating single-base mismatched sequences. Furthermore, analysis of diluted serum and cellular RNA samples demonstrated the preliminary applicability of the proposed strategy in biological matrices. The method provides a convenient, low-cost, and highly sensitive analytical platform for miRNA detection and bioanalytical research.

title: Application of Dual-Targeting Carbon Dot Nanozymes in Improving Hypoxia and Enhancing Small Interfering RNA-Mediated Gene Silencing for Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a malignant tumor with high morbidity and mortality, and current therapeutic effects remain unsatisfactory. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy has attracted widespread attention owing to its strong specificity and high silencing efficiency. Golgi apparatus (GA) protein 73 (GP73) is overexpressed in HCC and promotes proliferation and invasion of HCC. However, the hypoxic microenvironment of HCC facilitates GP73 synthesis. Based on the bidirectional regulation between GP73 and the hypoxic microenvironment, this study proposes the use of carbon dot nanozyme with dual-targeting properties to deliver GP73-siRNA to the GA of HCC cells, thereby inhibiting GP73 expression and simultaneously alleviating hypoxia for synergistic HCC treatment and improved efficacy. Specifically, GA targeting manganese-doped carbon dot nanozyme (Mn-CDs) was constructed using neutral red (with a large sp2 conjugated structure), L-cysteine (GA targeting agent), and manganese dioxide as raw materials via a one-step solvothermal method. Polyethyleneimine (PEI) and hyaluronic acid (HA) were modified on the surface of Mn-CDs to obtain the dual-targeting Mn-CDs-PEI-HA. Subsequently, Mn-CDs-PEI-HA was used as a carrier to load GP73-siRNA and form the Mn-CDs-PEI-HA/GP73-siRNA complex. Results demonstrated that the complex exhibited excellent catalase-like enzyme activity, which can alleviate tumor hypoxia, and could deliver GP73-siRNA to the GA of HCC cells, thereby silencing GP73 expression and synergistically inhibiting HCC progression. The therapeutic effect under hypoxic conditions was superior to that under normoxic conditions. Additionally, by simultaneously taking advantage of the favorable fluorescence and magnetic properties of Mn-CDs-PEI-HA, fluorescence/magnetic resonance dual-modality imaging of HCC was achieved, providing a new strategy for theranostics of HCC.

title: Comparative mitogenomics of Roscoea alpina and R. purpurea from contrasting elevations reveals mitochondrial genomic differentiation.
abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes are structurally dynamic and contribute to energy metabolism and stress responses. Comparative mitogenomic analyses of closely related species occupying contrasting elevations can provide insights into mitochondrial genomic differentiation across elevational environments. Using PacBio HiFi reads, we assembled and compared the mitochondrial genomes of the higher-altitude species R. alpina and the lower-altitude species R. purpurea. Both mitochondrial genome assemblies yielded graph-like structures, with R. alpina exhibiting a more complex assembly-graph topology, more dispersed repeats, and extensive evidence of dispersed-repeat-mediated recombination. Despite these structural differences, the two species retained broadly similar core gene complements, codon-usage patterns, and predicted RNA-editing profiles. Among genes represented by multiple annotated copies in both species, 12 had higher annotated copy numbers in R. alpina. Most shared protein-coding genes were highly conserved, whereas nad4 and rps3 each contained two nonsynonymous substitutions between the two species. Genes with higher annotated copy numbers and those showing limited sequence divergence were both annotated into respiratory complex I and mitochondrial translation. These results reveal pronounced differentiation in mitochondrial genome architecture alongside strong conservation of coding characteristics. Both the differences in gene representation and the limited sequence divergence converge on the same functional processes, suggesting a potential link between mitochondrial genomic changes and adaptation to high-altitude environments. We hypothesize that these genomic features may be relevant to the physiological performance of R. alpina in a high-altitude environment.

title: RNA vaccines in motion: A multidisciplinary exploration of design, delivery, and deployment.
abstract: RNA vaccines represent a major advance in prophylactic and therapeutic vaccinology, largely due to the success of nucleoside-modified mRNA vaccines encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) during the COVID-19 pandemic. These platforms build on long-standing progress in RNA chemistry, immunology, and nanotechnology. This review concentrates primarily on molecular design (codon/sequence optimization, chemical modifications, and data-driven antigen selection) and delivery optimization (LNPs and emerging alternatives like virus-like particles, extracellular vesicles, and ligand-targeted systems). Clinical progress is highlighted through examples from oncology, including personalized neoantigen approaches, combination therapies, and immunopeptidomics-guided validation, as well as early preclinical work on tolerance induction and localized protein replacement. Overall, continued refinement of RNA sequence engineering and delivery systems positions these platforms as flexible tools for rapid-response vaccination and therapy, especially where fast antigen adaptation and scalable production are required.

title: A host-virus arms race over FAM134B in African swine fever virus infection.
abstract: Although reticulophagy, the selective autophagy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), restricts several RNA viruses, whether this pathway constrains DNA virus infection remains unknown. Recently, we found that FAM134B (family with sequence similarity 134 member B), an ER-resident cargo receptor that mediates reticulophagy, restricts African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large cytoplasmic DNA virus, by targeting the major capsid proteins p72 and pA137R for lysosomal degradation, thereby blocking capsid assembly at perinuclear viral factories. ASFV counters this restriction through the virulence factor pMGF300-2 R encoded by the MGF300-2 R gene of ASFV, which binds to FAM134B, recruits LC3B (microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta), an ATG8 (autophagy-related protein 8) family member, via the C-terminal LC3-interacting region (LIR) motif, and directs FAM134B into autophagic degradation. Deletion of the MGF300-2 R gene in the ASFV genome restores FAM134B abundance, reduces viral replication, and attenuates virulence in pigs. These findings establish reticulophagy as a previously unrecognized antiviral barrier against a large DNA virus and reveal a host-virus arms race centered on the reticulophagy receptor.

title: Large mitogenome of Gunnera prorepens reveals extensive structural expansion alongside ancestral gene retention.
abstract: Gunnerales represent an early-diverging lineage sister to the Pentapetalae; however, mitochondrial genome evolution in this group remains uncharacterized. Characterizing the mitogenome structure and gene content in Gunnerales provides critical insights into early core eudicot evolution. We assembled and annotated the complete mitogenome of Gunnera prorepens using PacBio HiFi sequencing. The 1,374,480 bp genome, larger than those of many basal angiosperms and early-diverging eudicots. The coding gene set remains largely conserved, including 39 protein-coding genes, 23 unique tRNA genes, and three rRNA genes. The sdh3 and sdh4, which are frequently lost in other early-diverging eudicots, are retained. Genome expansion is primarily associated with repeat accumulation, including 1,066 dispersed repeats and several large inverted repeats that may represent potential recombination sites in the mitogenome. In addition, plastid-derived sequences account for 6.33% of the genome. We predicted 380 RNA editing sites, including an editing event predicted to restore the start codon of nad1. Comparative analyses indicate extensive structural rearrangements and genome expansion while maintaining an ancestral like coding gene complement. The mitogenome of G. prorepens provides additional evidence that mitochondrial genome expansion in angiosperms can occur without substantial loss of protein-coding genes. As a representative of Gunnerales, G. prorepens retains a largely ancestral mitochondrial gene complement despite its relatively large genome size. Our results underscore that significant mitogenomic expansion and ancestral gene retention can be uncoupled during the early divergence of core eudicots.

title: Discovery of direct-acting small-molecule RIG-I agonists through creation of a selective CARD activation platform.
abstract: Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) plays a pivotal role in recognizing and combating RNA viruses in humans, and it has become a drug target of significant interest. RIG-I agonists composed of dsRNA represent antiviral and antitumor therapies, however the development of small-molecule RIG-I agonists, with their potential for improved pharmacokinetics, remains an unmet need. Here, we report small-molecule RIG-I agonists that directly activate the RIG-I receptor protein. These agonists stimulate the first step in RIG-I signaling by triggering release of the signaling domains (CARDs) from an autorepressed form of the protein. This was achieved by developing a sensitive high-throughput screening (HTS) assay that directly monitors CARD expulsion through optical methods. The resulting screen hits were refined and optimized, leading to a specific RIG-I agonist that induces a robust interferon response. This study establishes a pharmacophore and assay for development of small molecules that precisely modulate RIG-I signaling.

title: HPLC-UV-Guided Discovery of Penicitrinoids A-K and the Structure Revision of Fusariumin B: 3,4-seco-Spiromeroterpenoids from the Marine-Derived Fungus Penicillium citrinum F5025.
abstract: Eleven previously undescribed 3,4-seco-spiromeroterpenoids, penicitrinoids A-K (1-11), one revised analogue (12), and three known compounds (13-15) were isolated under HPLC-UV guidance from the marine-derived fungus Penicillium citrinum F5025. Their structures and absolute configurations were unequivocally determined through HR-ESIMS, extensive 1D and 2D NMR analysis, ECD calculations, and a single-crystal X-ray diffraction study. Notably, Penicitrinoid A (1) represents the first example of a 3,4-seco-spiromeroterpenoid incorporating a tetrahydrofuran ring. Moreover, the previously reported structure of fusariumin B was revised and corresponds to compound 12. In antiviral assays, compounds 8 and 14 exhibited activity against influenza virus (strain ZX1109) with EC50 values of 6.41 and 10.91 μM, respectively. Compound 8 also showed activity against Ross River virus (RRV) (EC50 = 51.92 μM), while compound 10 was active against dengue virus (DENV-2) (EC50 = 51.91 μM). Mechanistic studies indicated that the antiviral effects of compounds 8 and 10 against RRV and DENV-2 are primarily mediated through interference with viral RNA replication. This study not only expands the structural diversity of 3,4-seco-spiromeroterpenoids but also provides a foundation for their development as potential antiviral agents.

title: The unfolded protein response as a proteotoxic stress-resolution circuit: branch-selective signaling and failed resolution in environmental immunotoxicity.
abstract: Environmental immunotoxicity is commonly framed through oxidative stress, cytotoxicity, inflammation, receptor-mediated signaling and cell- or tissue-specific mechanisms. This review proposes that proteotoxic stress resolution represents an additional layer linking environmental exposure to immune dysfunction. Specifically, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is considered as a branch-selective proteotoxic stress-resolution circuit that can shape immune outcomes when endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis is perturbed. The framework is offered as a hypothesis-generating conceptual structure rather than an established mechanistic paradigm, and the causal step linking failed resolution to immune dysfunction remains largely extrapolated from non-toxicological ER-stress models. Evidence from ER proteostasis biology, immune-cell function and toxicology indicates that environmental toxicants can disrupt protein folding, ER calcium balance, redox homeostasis, lipid composition, degradation pathways and secretory load, thereby engaging distinct combinations of IRE1α, PERK and ATF6 signaling. These branches generate immune-relevant outputs: IRE1α links ER stress to RNA processing and inflammatory signaling, PERK controls translational suppression and fate selection, and ATF6 supports restoration of folding capacity and secretory competence. Across macrophages, dendritic cells, T cells, plasma cells and barrier epithelial cells, immune outcomes depend on branch bias, signaling duration, cell-type context and resolution through ER-associated degradation, autophagy, ER-phagy, translational recovery and restoration of calcium and redox balance. This framework predicts that repeated low-dose exposures, mixed toxicant inputs and incomplete post-exposure recovery can shift immune or barrier cells into inflammatory, suppressive or barrier-disruptive states without overt cytotoxicity. It also supports time-resolved, branch-specific and cell-specific profiling for immunotoxic risk assessment.

title: Betaine alleviates renal osteodystrophy by stabilizing ABCG1 mRNA to inhibit HMOX1-mediated ferroptosis in BMSCs.
abstract: Renal osteodystrophy is a debilitating complication of chronic kidney disease characterized by deteriorated bone microarchitecture and impaired bone formation, leading to increased fracture risk. Despite the pressing need for anabolic therapies, the cellular mechanisms by which uremic stress compromises osteoprogenitor function remain poorly defined. Here, metabolomic profiling of renal osteodystrophy patient cohorts revealed a profound depletion of circulating betaine. We show that betaine supplementation not only rescued the osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells challenged with the uremic toxin indoxyl sulfate but also ameliorated skeletal deterioration in a rat model of chronic kidney disease. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that indoxyl sulfate triggered ferroptosis in bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells-characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and aberrant HMOX1 up-regulation-thereby arresting osteogenesis. Betaine mitigates this ferroptotic stress through a novel post-transcriptional mechanism. Specifically, betaine down-regulated the RNA-binding protein hnRNP A1, preventing the recruitment of the CNOT1 deadenylase complex. This inhibition stabilized Abcg1 mRNA, leading to restored ABCG1 expression. Functional perturbation studies confirmed that the ABCG1-HMOX1 axis was indispensable for the anti-ferroptotic and osteoprotective effects of betaine. Collectively, our findings delineate a Betaine-hnRNP A1/CNOT1-ABCG1-HMOX1 signaling cascade that links metabolic deficiency to ferroptosis-driven osteogenic failure, positioning betaine as a promising anabolic therapeutic strategy for renal osteodystrophy.

title: Djcoronin controls the AP axis polarity through Wnt signaling pathway during planarian regeneration.
abstract: Planarians have whole body regeneration ability and are model animals for the study of regeneration and development. Coronin is an actin binding protein involved in a variety of cellular processes. However, the precise role of coronins in tissue regeneration remains unclear. In this study, we found that Djcoronin exhibited a concentration gradient expression pattern throughout the worm and was highly expressed in the newly formed tail region after amputation. We used RNA interference to knockdown Djcoronin and found that loss of Djcoronin function affected tail regeneration, characterized by nervous system defects and a two-headed phenotype, while having no significant effect on head regeneration. Importantly, knockdown of Djcoronin downregulated the expression of β-catenin and posterior Wnt genes, accompanied with the reversal of the head-tail polarity. Moreover, treatment with Wnt agonist 1 significantly alleviated the regeneration and polarity defects caused by Djcoronin knockdown. In conclusion, our study suggests that Djcoronin is an important regulator of polarity maintenance that contributes to AP polarity regulation via the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.

title: Multi-omics Profiling Reveals the Effects of Xihuangcao on Hepatic Fibrosis Attenuation through Gut Microbiota and Metabolic Reprogramming.
abstract: In various chronic liver diseases, hepatic fibrosis represents a frequent pathological event. This process involves the activation of hepatic stellate cells, along with the consequent excessive deposition of extracellular matrix. Emerging evidence highlights the contribution of gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal barrier dysfunction to its progression, underscoring the potential of targeting the liver-gut axis. Xihuangcao, a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used for acute cholecystitis and jaundice hepatitis, exhibits antifibrotic activity, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, hepatic fibrosis models were established to evaluate the antifibrotic effects of 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao (Isodon lophanthoides (Buch.-Ham. ex D.Don) H.Hara, Isodon lophanthoides var. graciliflorus (Benth.) H.Hara, and Isodon serra Kudô) through integrating histopathological, transcriptomics, metabolomics, 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing, and network pharmacology analyses. The results indicated that all 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao markedly alleviated hepatic fibrosis and reduced collagen deposition. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Xihuangcao down-regulated profibrotic mediators (Toll-like receptor 5, transforming growth factor-β, and platelet-derived growth factor) and modulated mitogen-activated protein kinase, steroid biosynthesis, bile secretion, and retinol metabolism pathways, highlighting its coordinated suppression of inflammation-driven fibrogenic activation in hepatic fibrosis. Liver metabolomics revealed Xihuangcao's effect on restoration of energy metabolism, amino acid turnover, and redox homeostasis. Xihuangcao also corrected fibrosis-induced gut dysbiosis, characterized by reduced Verrucomicrobia and increased S24-7 abundance, while suppressing pathogenic genera such as Clostridium and Prevotella. Moreover, Xihuangcao decreased profibrotic metabolites (androstan-3α,17β-diol) and suppressed choline-related metabolic pathways associated with fibrogenic signaling. Network pharmacology and experimental validation further identified PI3K/Akt inhibition as a key mechanism suppressing hepatic stellate cell activation. In summary, this study, based on integrative multi-omics analyses (metabolomics, transcriptomics, and 16S rRNA sequencing), found that Xihuangcao alleviates liver fibrosis by modulating inflammatory responses, metabolic disorders, and gut microbiota dysbiosis via the gut-liver axis. Furthermore, network pharmacology combined with in vitro experiments revealed that inhibition of hepatic stellate cell activation through the PI3K/Akt pathway may be the critical mechanism underlying its therapeutic efficacy.

title: A coculture system of Epicoccum nigrum with Mucor racemosus induces red pigment biosynthesis in vinegar mash.
abstract: Fungal pigments hold significant food industrial value due to their safe and sustainable properties. Here we identified a naturally occurring coculture pair Epicoccum nigrum SPDX618 and Mucor racemosus SPDX522 in vinegar mash that produced red pigments, which was not observed in either monoculture. Our results showed that E. nigrum acted as the pigment producer while M. racemosus served as the elicitor. Response surface methodology and pH stabilization strategy improved the yield of red pigment into 328.7 U/g. Through bioactivity-guided fractionation coupled with UHPLC-MS/MS and in silico structure reconstitution, four red pigments were preliminarily assigned as anthracycline-like compounds. RNA-seq analysis revealed a putative dual-PKS gene cluster (SPDX618009169-SPDX618009178) with exclusively upregulation in cocultured E. nigrum that is potentially involved in red pigment biosynthesis. Besides, the production of the yellow pigment epipyrone was reduced in cocultured E. nigrum, consistent with the downregulated transcription level of its biosynthesis genes. Comparative metabolomics analysis further revealed a broad downregulation in both of primary metabolism and secondary metabolism in coculture system, indicating that a competition interaction relationship also existed between E. nigrum and M. racemosus. Altogether, this study reports a fungal coculture system that exhibited red pigments production. These findings contribute to the understanding of microbial interaction-driven metabolite biosynthesis and may provide a foundation for future exploration of their potential application as a colorant. KEY POINTS: • An Epicoccum nigrum-Mucor racemosus coculture system was identified to produce red pigment for the first time. • E. nigrum acts as the red pigment producer and M. racemosus serves as the elicitor. • RNA-seq analysis tentatively identified a putative dual-PKS gene cluster upregulated in coculture that is putatively involved in red pigment biosynthesis.

title: Acupotomy Alleviates Pain and Attenuates Spinal Neuronal Hyperexcitability in Knee Osteoarthritis Rats: Implication of the CaMKII/GluA1 Axis.
abstract: To investigate the spinal mechanisms underlying the analgesic effects of acupotomy on chronic pain and central sensitization in rats with monosodium iodoacetate (MIA)-induced knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Following MIA-induced KOA and a three-week acupotomy intervention in rats, pain behaviors and joint pathology were assessed. Spinal RNA-sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. Key targets (CaMKII and GluA1) were validated at both mRNA and protein levels using RT-qPCR and Western blotting. Furthermore, immunofluorescence and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology were employed to evaluate the activation and excitability of spinal substantia gelatinosa (SG) neurons. Acupotomy significantly alleviated mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia and reduced joint degeneration in KOA rats. RNA-seq analysis revealed the modulation of 220 genes in the spinal cord. These DEGs were significantly enriched in calcium signaling and synaptic transmission pathways, highlighting CaMKII and Gria1 as potential key molecules. Molecular validations confirmed that acupotomy downregulated CaMKII and Gria1 mRNA expression and the phosphorylation ratios of CaMKII and GluA1. Furthermore, acupotomy reduced the activation of p-CaMKII-positive neurons in the spinal SG region and dampened their abnormally high-frequency action potential discharges. Acupotomy intervention ameliorates peripheral joint degeneration and exerts significant analgesia in KOA, which is accompanied by a reduction in the intrinsic hyperexcitability of spinal SG neurons. Although direct causal validation utilizing targeted inhibitors is warranted, our findings suggest that this analgesic effect is closely associated with the downregulation of the CaMKII/GluA1 signaling axis, providing a plausible central mechanistic framework.

title: Oliceridine and morphine differentially modulate the gut microbiota-intestinal barrier axis in a rat postoperative pain model.
abstract: Oliceridine is a novel G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist with potentially improved gastrointestinal tolerability compared with conventional opioids. However, its impact on postoperative intestinal homeostasis-specifically the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier-remains poorly understood. A postoperative pain model was established in male Sprague-Dawley rats using the Brennan plantar incision method. Animals were randomly assigned to four groups: non-incision control (CON), plantar incision plus normal saline, plantar incision plus oliceridine (OLI, 1 mg/kg subcutaneous bolus followed by continuous infusion at 1 mg/kg/day for 72 h), and plantar incision plus morphine (MF, 5 mg/kg subcutaneous bolus followed by continuous infusion at 5 mg/kg/day for 72 h). Analgesic efficacy was assessed by mechanical withdrawal threshold (MWT) and area under the curve (AUC). Intestinal morphology, epithelial Claudin-1 expression by immunofluorescence (n = 4 per group), gut microbiota composition (16S rRNA gene sequencing, n = 6 per group), and host ileal transcriptomic profiles (RNA-seq, n = 3 per group) were evaluated. Oliceridine and morphine produced comparable analgesia, as reflected by MWT AUC (P < 0.0001 vs. NS; OLI vs. MF: P = 0.8770). Both opioids alleviated postoperative mechanical hypersensitivity. Compared with NS, opioid treatment increased the relative abundance of Limosilactobacillus and Lactobacillus and decreased Streptococcus. Exploratory microbiome analysis identified a potential Lactobacillus-related signal, but no genus-level difference between the OLI and MF groups remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Transcriptomic analysis revealed distinct ileal gene-expression profiles between the OLI and MF groups. Relative to MF, OLI was associated with higher expression of genes related to epithelial barrier integrity and brush border function and lower expression of genes involved in immune-related pathways. Histologically, both opioids attenuated intestinal injury compared with NS, with no significant difference between OLI and MF. In contrast, relative Claudin-1 fluorescence intensity was significantly higher in the OLI group than in the MF group (P = 0.036), providing protein-level support for the barrier-related transcriptomic findings. Integrated correlation analysis identified associations between Lactobacillus-related taxa and host genes linked to barrier function and metabolism (|r| > 0.6, P < 0.01). Oliceridine and morphine produced comparable analgesia. Exploratory microbiome analysis identified a potential Lactobacillus-related signal, but no genus-level differences remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Oliceridine was associated with a distinct ileal transcriptomic profile and higher Claudin-1 fluorescence intensity than morphine, although histological injury did not differ between the two groups. The functional significance of these molecular differences requires further investigation.

title: EZH2 in Ovarian Cancer: Mechanistic Dependencies, Therapeutic Platforms and Translational Combinations.
abstract: Ovarian cancer remains the deadliest gynecologic malignancy because most patients present with advanced disease and ultimately relapse despite surgery, platinum- based chemotherapy, and modern maintenance strategies. Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), the catalytic core of polycomb repressive complex 2, has emerged as a context-dependent epigenetic regulator that links chromatin repression to cellular plasticity, repair-state adaptation, stemness, metabolism, and immune remodeling. This review aims to define the clinical relevance of context-dependent EZH2 states in ovarian cancer and compare the therapeutic logic, evidence maturity, and limitations of available EZH2-targeting platforms. We conducted a focused narrative synthesis of ovarian-cancer-relevant preclinical studies, medicinal-chemistry reports, and clinical evidence, supplemented by targeted PubMed searches and ClinicalTrials.gov checks during revision. Evidence was interpreted in light of biologic context, therapeutic platform, combination rationale, and the degree of ovarian-specific clinical support. Current evidence supports a role for EZH2 in ovarian tumor progression through canonical polycomb repressive complex 2-dependent mechanisms and, in selected contexts, non-canonical functions. Therapeutic development now includes catalytic inhibitors, dual EZH1/2 inhibitors, EEDdirected inhibitors, degraders, and RNA-based strategies. In ovarian cancer, the strongest mechanistic rationale currently supports combinations with platinum chemotherapy and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition, whereas immune-oriented and broader cotargeting strategies remain promising but less mature. The key translational question is not simply whether EZH2 can be pharmacologically engaged, but which form of EZH2 dependency is present, in which biologic context, and with which partner therapy. Catalytic inhibition alone may underperform when adaptive redundancy, polycomb complex architecture, or non-canonical protein function sustain tumor fitness. EZH2 should be viewed not as a uniformly validated ovarian-cancer target, but as a context-dependent vulnerability whose most defensible near-term clinical positioning is biomarkerinformed combination development rather than unselected monotherapy.

title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time.Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

title: Quantitative Analysis Reveals IL-17A Widens Nasal Epithelial Tight Junction Gaps via AMPK in Allergic Rhinitis.
abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a chronic IgE-mediated inflammatory disease characterized by nasal epithelial barrier dysfunction. Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) has been implicated in epithelial barrier disruption, but its role in regulating nasal epithelial tight junctions (TJs) remains unclear. To investigate the effects of IL-17A on nasal epithelial TJs integrity and determine whether adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling mediates IL-17A-induced barrier dysfunction in AR. Inferior turbinate tissues from patients with AR and healthy controls were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy, quantitative PCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Human nasal epithelial cells cultured at an air-liquid interface were stimulated with IL-17A for 28 days. TJs integrity was assessed by transepithelial electrical resistance, fluorescein isothiocyanate-dextran permeability, and automated ImageJ-based quantification of TJs morphology. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed, and AMPK activity was modulated using AICAR and Compound C. AR tissues exhibited disrupted TJs and suppressed AMPK activity. IL-17A expression was elevated and negatively correlated with TJs protein levels. In human nasal epithelial cells, IL-17A reduced TJs protein expression, decreased transepithelial electrical resistance, increased paracellular permeability, and widened intercellular spaces. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated suppression of AMPK signaling after IL-17A stimulation. Activation of AMPK with AICAR restored TJs expression and improved barrier function. IL-17A impairs nasal epithelial barrier integrity by inhibiting AMPK signaling, whereas AMPK activation rescues TJs structure and function, identifying the IL-17A/AMPK axis as a potential therapeutic target in allergic rhinitis.

title: Genetic prioritization and functional characterization of macrophage TXNDC17 in Ischemic heart disease.
abstract: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) still works as the leading cause of mortality through the world. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress is a key player in the pathogenesis of IHD. However, the potential mechanisms and key regulatory factors remain not fully clear. In our research, single-cell RNA sequencing data were integrated with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) and colocalization analyses, aimed at systematically recognizing ER stress-related genes associated with IHD and to evaluate genetically predicted associations with IHD. The selected candidate was subsequently examined using single-cell expression analysis and in vitro experiments involving pro-inflammatory THP-1 macrophage-like cells and AC16 cardiomyocytes. Cytokine expression in macrophages was assessed by quantitative PCR, whereas cytokine concentrations in OGD-conditioned medium were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Recipient-cell ER-stress and ferroptosis-associated responses were evaluated using molecular, biochemical and pharmacological rescue assays. A total of 2564 genes associated with both IHD and ER stress were identified, enriched in pathways related to oxidative stress, protein folding, and apoptotic signalling. Integrative SMR, colocalization and Mendelian randomization analyses identified a genetically predicted inverse association between TXNDC17 expression and IHD risk, thereby prioritizing TXNDC17 for subsequent functional investigation. Pseudotemporal analysis revealed a dynamic alteration in TXNDC17 expression during myeloid cell development, with an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease. Experimental validation revealed that TXNDC17 was highly expressed in myeloid cells and that its knockdown in macrophages aggravated OGD-induced injury, increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production and release, and increased apoptosis-associated injury. OGD-conditioned medium from TXNDC17-silenced macrophages further promoted ER stress- and ferroptosis-associated injury in cardiomyocytes. Genetically predicted TXNDC17 expression was inversely associated with IHD risk. Functional experiments further implicated macrophage TXNDC17 in regulating inflammatory conditioned-medium-mediated cardiomyocyte injury, although its causal relevance to IHD in vivo remains to be established.

title: CCKBR signalling controls human definitive endoderm specification and pancreatic lineage differentiation.
abstract: Paracrine signalling by hormone-producing endocrine cells potentially influences pancreatic development, but this feedback regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the roles of gastrin (GAST), cholecystokinin (CCK) and their receptor cholecystokinin B receptor (CCKBR) during human pancreatic development. Human iPSCs were differentiated stepwise into definitive endoderm and then the pancreatic endocrine lineage. To assess CCKBR function, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate CCKBR-knockout iPSC lines. We profiled transcriptional states by bulk and single-cell RNA-seq with computational analyses, and complemented these with biochemical assays, flow cytometry (FACS) and confocal microscopy. CCKBR expression peaked during definitive endoderm formation and progressively declined during differentiation, remaining detectable in pancreatic progenitors but largely absent from the endocrine lineage. By contrast, GAST and CCK were expressed only transiently during pancreatic progenitor and endocrine lineage formation. Pharmacological activation/inhibition and genetic knockout implicated CCKBR signalling during definitive endoderm formation. Consistently, bulk RNA-seq indicated that CCKBR deletion triggered ectodermal- and mesodermal-associated transcriptional programs and diminished pancreatic lineage specification. During pancreatic induction and lineage formation, sustained CCKBR activation with GAST or CCK attenuated endocrinogenesis and promoted epithelial structure formation. Further analysis revealed the emergence of a pancreatic ductal-like cell formation under prolonged CCKBR stimulation. This study provides mechanistic evidence that the GAST/CCK-CCKBR axis is functionally important during human endoderm and pancreas development. This pathway is repeatedly required during in vitro pluripotent stem cell differentiation, regulating germ-layer formation as well as ductal vs endocrine fate decisions. These findings support the optimisation of pancreatic differentiation protocols and inform future studies on whether this axis contributes to human pancreas development and disease.

title: Beyond chaperoning: HSPA8 modulates alternative splicing of PPP2R2D to drive apoptotic evasion and macrophage-associated immune microenvironment remodeling in triple-negative breast cancer.
abstract: The molecular chaperone HSPA8 is classically recognized for its role in protein homeostasis, and while its upregulation correlates with poor prognosis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), whether HSPA8 exerts non-canonical functions beyond chaperoning remains unknown. Through integrative transcriptomic profiling, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), isoform-specific rescue experiments, and in vivo xenograft models, we investigated the functional and mechanistic role of HSPA8 in TNBC pathogenesis. We unveil a paradigm-shifting function for HSPA8 as a modulator of alternative splicing of the PP2A regulatory subunit gene PPP2R2D, promoting exon 2 retention to favor the full-length PPP2R2D-2 isoform over the truncated PPP2R2D-1. These two isoforms exhibit functionally distinct roles: only PPP2R2D-2 possesses pro-survival activity, whereas PPP2R2D-1 lacks this function. Specifically, PPP2R2D-2 rescues HSPA8 depletion-induced apoptosis by modulating the mitochondrial pathway (BAX/BCL-2/cleaved Caspase-3) and restores in vivo tumor growth. Strikingly, this splicing axis also correlates with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by altered M1/M2 macrophage marker abundance. These findings uncover a dual mechanism that simultaneously drives intrinsic survival signaling and is associated with alterations in the tumor immune microenvironment. They transcend the classical chaperone paradigm by establishing HSPA8 as a non-canonical splicing modulator, and the HSPA8-PPP2R2D-2 axis emerges as a critical vulnerability in TNBC, offering a novel therapeutic angle that concurrently targets tumor cell survival and microenvironmental immunosuppression.

title: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that TAF7 promotes colorectal cancer stemness by targeting SOX2.
abstract: Cancer cell stemness plays a decisive role in tumor metastasis and recurrence. TATA-box binding protein-associated factor 7 (TAF7), which is highly expressed in multiple cancers and critical for metastasis, has not been clearly linked to stemness characteristics in colorectal cancer (CRC). Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the role of TAF7 in CRC stemness. Differential gene expression and associated signaling pathways were screened using single-cell transcriptomic data from CRC and adjacent normal tissues obtained from the GEO database and validated in CRC cells. A TAF7-knockdown CRC cell line was established to assess the impact of TAF7 on tumor cell stemness. The molecular mechanism of TAF7 in regulating CRC stemness was explored through bioinformatics analysis combined with chromatin immunoprecipitation and dual-luciferase reporter assays and validated by rescue experiments. Finally, a CRC xenograft mouse model was established to examine the effect of targeting TAF7 on tumor cell stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Re-analysis of single-cell transcriptomics data identified a TAF7+ epithelial cell subpopulation that is highly expressed in CRC and characteristically expresses the stemness marker SOX2. In vitro experiments demonstrated that high TAF7 expression promotes CRC stemness, primarily by enhancing the transcriptional activation of SOX2. Rescue experiments confirmed that targeting the TAF7/SOX2 axis suppresses CRC stemness and EMT. Furthermore, in vivo experiments showed that TAF7 targeting inhibits tumor growth and CRC stemness in mice. Our integrated single-cell transcriptomic and functional analyses reveal that TAF7 promotes CRC stemness and EMT progression via transcriptional activation of the stemness marker SOX2.

title: Exploratory chromosome 14-focused transcriptomic profiling of PSEN1-associated familial Alzheimer's disease across brain regions.
abstract: Familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) is an inherited form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease associated with pathogenic variants in presenilin 1 (PSEN1). To explore chromosome 14-associated transcriptional patterns in FAD across anatomically distinct brain regions, publicly available RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) datasets from frontal cortex, temporal cortex, and whole-brain samples were analyzed. Because one FAD sample and one control sample were available for each brain region, expression differences were evaluated descriptively using observed log₂ fold-change values rather than conventional inferential differential-expression statistics. Functional annotation and protein-protein interaction analyses were subsequently used to provide biological context for the observed expression patterns. Distinct regional expression patterns were observed within the chromosome 14-focused dataset. Higher expression was observed for representative genes including FITM1, IFI27, AHSA1, and NFKBIA in the frontal cortex, and DHRS4L2, ESR2, GPR65, EFCAB11, and HOMEZ in the temporal cortex. The observed expression patterns were associated with inflammatory, cellular stress, metabolic, receptor-mediated, proteostatic, and neuronal signaling-related functions. Network analysis was used to contextualize these expression patterns rather than to infer causal regulatory relationships. Five representative proteins-NFKBIA, ESR2, GPR65, AHSA1, and IFI27-were further examined structural information to provide structural context for selected transcriptomic observations. Given the absence of biological replication and the chromosome 14-focused design, these findings should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Independent replicated cohorts and complementary transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional studies are required to determine the reproducibility and biological relevance of the observed patterns.

title: Integrated Single-Myofibre Multi-Omics Correlates Inflammatory State to Myosin Energetics in ICU-Acquired Weakness.
abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy is a pervasive complication of critical illness that worsens survival and recovery, yet remains poorly explained by current clinical or molecular markers. To directly connect disease-associated molecular states to the contractile machinery, this study combined sequential functional, transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of the same single human skeletal myofibres from critically ill patients in the intensive care unit with acquired weakness (ICU-AW) and controls. This integrated approach provides a framework for validating molecular signals directly within the cellular and biomechanical context. Differential expression analyses between control and ICU-AW myofibres show marked donor-level heterogeneity, with no differentially expressed features (FDR < 0.05). Ranked gene set enrichment analyses revealed distinct transcriptional and proteomic signatures between conditions, as well as a subtle yet conserved myofibre state enriched in ICU-AW, characterised by inflammatory and chemotactic gene programmes, intracellular structural remodelling and bioenergetic adaptation. Nineteen features were significantly (FDR < 0.05) altered at both RNA and protein levels from the same myofibre. Overall, these 19 overlapping features link an inflammatory transcriptional landscape to a proteomic shift toward mitochondrial and translational machinery, revealing a coordinated stress-adaptation programme with selective post-translational control in fibres from patients with ICU-AW. Further integration with the functional dataset revealed fibres in this state displayed selectively disrupted myosin dynamics, evidenced by prolonged ATP turnover time of myosin heads in their super-relaxed conformation, suggesting altered myosin energetics as a contributor to muscle dysfunction. These findings define a discrete, disease-associated myofibre state and validate a proof-of-concept integrative single-fibre framework for connecting multi-omic heterogeneity to molecular motor function in complex human disease. The identification of coordinated transcriptomic and proteomic programmes, validated through functional measurement, suggests that targeting this fibre state may offer new therapeutic opportunities in ICU-acquired dysfunction and related muscle disorders.

title: Transcriptomics analysis and experimental assay to screen prognostic genes of N6-methyladenosine RNA methylation related to cuproptosis in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Cuproptosis and N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation have been identified as significant factors in cancer. Consequently, we seek to uncover m6A RNA methylation-related prognostic genes that are correlated with cuproptosis-related genes (CRGs) in colorectal cancer (CRC) and develop an effective prognostic model. Based on public datasets, differential expression analysis, correlation analysis, and machine learning were conducted to identify prognostic genes. Subsequently, a prognostic model was constructed and validated. Furthermore, independent predictive markers were found through the use of clinical characteristics and risk score, to establish a prognostic nomogram. Prognostic gene expression in CRC and normal samples was evaluated using reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). According to the prognostic genes, potential drugs for CRC were predicted using artificial intelligence drug design (AIDD) and computer-aided drug design (CADD). A prognostic model was developed utilizing 7 m6A RNA methylation-related prognostic genes that were significantly correlated with CRGs (MMP1, TIMP1, SNAI1, CDC25C, XRN2, COX5A, and FBXL5) in CRC. Survival analysis uncovered a notable contrast in survival outcomes between the high- and low-risk groups. The nomogram constructed based on age, stage, T stage, and risk scores demonstrated good predictive ability. RT-qPCR results showed that MMP1, TIMP1, SNAI1, and CDC25C were upregulated in CRC samples, while COX5A was downregulated, consistent with the bioinformatics analysis results. Furthermore, 186 candidate drugs targeting COX5A were identified, 153 of which showed better predicted binding affinity than the positive-control ligand 3,5‑diiodo‑L‑thyronine. Our analysis sets the groundwork for a more comprehensive comprehension of the fundamental molecular pathways involved in CRC.

title: Interpretable machine learning prioritizes transcriptomic features associated with ferroptosis-mitochondrial permeability transition net activity states in cervical cancer.
abstract: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated cervical carcinogenesis involves oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and altered non-apoptotic cell-death programs. Ferroptosis and mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT)-driven necrosis may share upstream stress-related transcriptional signals, but their joint pathway-state features in cervical cancer remain incompletely characterized. We constructed a directionality-aware net pathway activity framework using evidence-audited ferroptosis-promoting, ferroptosis-inhibitory, MPT-promoting, and MPT-inhibitory gene sets in 304 TCGA-CESC primary tumors. The score was benchmarked against ssGSEA, GSVA, and PLAGE and evaluated in controlled simulations. For feature prioritization, score-defining genes were excluded from predictors and Elastic Net feature selection, XGBoost tuning, and model fitting were performed strictly within repeated nested cross-validation. Outer-test SHAP, model-sensitivity analysis, and a 200-permutation complete-pipeline test were used for interpretation and robustness assessment. External validation used GSE138080, GSE63514, GSE223804, and GSE151666. CombinedNet showed moderate-to-high concordance with ssGSEA, GSVA, and PLAGE (Spearman rho = 0.735, 0.882, and 0.943, respectively), while 1,300 controlled simulations showed strong recovery of the latent promoter-minus-inhibitor balance across scenarios and effect sizes (mean rho = 0.944; mean sign-recovery accuracy = 0.902; mean standardized RMSE = 0.305). The leakage-resistant repeated nested-CV model yielded AUC = 0.780 (95% CI 0.766-0.795); a matched complete-pipeline permutation test gave empirical p = 0.005. Stability-weighted SHAP and perturbation prioritized CKMT1B and KLK13, whereas GNA13, PANX2, and all five sterol genes were not selected in any of 25 outer-fold models. The sterol genes retained modest score correlations but showed no model sensitivity. Across three lesion-progression cohorts, no pathway score remained associated with stage after FDR correction; in the cancer-only GSE151666 RNA-seq cohort, CombinedNet also showed no FIGO-stage trend. This study supports directionality-aware transcriptomic scoring and a leakage-resistant feature-prioritization framework, but does not support GNA13/PANX2 or cholesterol-biosynthesis signals as stable model drivers or the composite score as a validated lesion-stage biomarker. The findings remain hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.

title: Integrated genetic and functional analyses reveal the pathogenic effects of a novel STXBP3 variant in very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease with immunodeficiency.
abstract: Very early onset inflammatory bowel disease (VEOIBD) is frequently driven by monogenic defects. Pathogenic variants in the syntaxin-binding protein 3 (STXBP3) gene have been implicated in VEOIBD; however, the relationship between specific variant types and clinical manifestations remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify the genetic cause in a patient with VEOIBD and explore the possible genotype-phenotype correlations of STXBP3-related disorders. We performed trio-whole-exome sequencing (trio-WES) on a male infant presenting with VEOIBD, sensorineural hearing loss, and immunodeficiency. Functional consequences of the identified variant were investigated using RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), western blotting and co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assay. A systematic literature review was conducted to analyze clinical features and inheritance patterns across all reported STXBP3 cases. A novel heterozygous splice-site variant in STXBP3 (c.1022_1029 + 3del) was identified. RNA-seq and RT-PCR confirmed that this variant causes aberrant splicing, leading to the skipping of exon 12 and the production of a truncated protein. Co-IP showed that the aberrant protein reduced the ability to bind STX4. The comprehensive analysis of 13 patients revealed possible genotype-phenotype correlations: splice-site and frameshift variants were observed predominantly follow an autosomal dominant (AD) pattern associated with VEOIBD, sensorineural hearing loss, and immunodeficiency; conversely, missense variants generally follow an autosomal recessive (AR) pattern linked to VEOIBD, and congenital malformations. Given the small cohort, these comparisons were descriptive and were not intended to establish definitive genotype-phenotype associations. We identified a novel pathogenic STXBP3 variant and validated its impact on its function. The observed differences between AD and AR cases provided a preliminary, hypothesis-generating framework for understanding STXBP3-related disease, which require validation in larger cohorts.

title: Decoding radiation-induced transcriptomic signatures of human leukocytes using long-read RNA-seq: clinical and biodosimetric implications.
abstract: Gene expression profiling in radiation-exposed blood is a valuable tool for biodosimetry and clinical research. Evaluating the blood's transcriptomic radiation response provides insight into absorbed dose, hematotoxicities, and immune reactions. However, detailed analysis using long-read RNA sequencing is currently limited in its diffusion, despite the potential additional insights that could be extracted, including novel isoform discovery and on-the-field gene expression studies, owing to its portability. In this study, we utilized Oxford Nanopore Technologies' long-read RNA sequencing on human peripheral blood leukocytes from three healthy donors 6 h after exposure of whole peripheral blood to 4 Gy of X-rays. Compared to sham-irradiated (0 Gy) blood samples, gene-level differential expression analysis identified 117 upregulated and 66 downregulated genes, including canonical DNA damage repair and inflammatory responses. At the transcript level, 102 transcripts were significantly upregulated, and 17 were downregulated, revealing isoform-specific regulation that was not captured at the gene level. Notably, IL32, which was not detected as significantly changed at the gene level, exhibited significant upregulation of two transcript isoforms (log2 fold-changes of 1.19 and 1.99), while WDR74, ITM2B, AK2, and RPS19 displayed changes in transcript usage following irradiation. Leveraging long-read RNA sequencing, we further identified novel candidate isoforms, including protein-coding isoforms of PHPT1 and FBXO22 as well as non-coding candidates. Notably, the FBXO22 isoform showed evidence of altered protein domain architecture relative to the reference isoform. This study is the first to systematically investigate differential transcript usage in the leukocyte fraction of irradiated human whole blood using long-read RNA sequencing. We confirmed known radiation-response signatures at the gene level and identified transcript-level regulatory events and novel candidate isoforms that can be masked in gene-level analyses and conventional short-read pipelines. These findings demonstrate the potential of long-read RNA sequencing to provide a more detailed view of radiation-induced transcriptomic alterations, with potential applications in biodosimetry and clinical settings.

title: A single-cell atlas of intracranial aneurysm progression identifies a dysfunctional VSMC subpopulation associated with rupture risk.
abstract: Intracranial aneurysm (IA) rupture is a life-threatening event. While inflammation is implicated, the cellular mechanisms associated with progression from stable lesion to rupture remain poorly defined at single-cell resolution. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on a mouse model spanning sham, formed, and ruptured IA stages. Computational analyses included trajectory inference, cell-cell communication analysis, and metabolic scoring. Key findings were validated using human IA bulk RNA-seq data and protein-level assays on matched clinical tissues. Our single-cell atlas revealed a progressive "inflammatory-lytic" microenvironment marked by immune cell infiltration and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) depletion. We identified a metabolically specialized VSMC subpopulation (VSMC_0) that was selectively lost in formed and ruptured aneurysms. Pseudotime analysis indicated VSMC differentiation blockade, associated with downregulation of the structural genes actin alpha2, smooth muscle (ACTA2) and prolyl 4-hydroxylase subunit alpha2 (P4HA2), which correlated with irregular aneurysm shape a strong clinical predictor of rupture risk. Cell communication analysis positioned VSMC_0 as a signaling hub to macrophages, suggesting a feed-forward inflammatory loop. These findings were validated in human IAs tissues. Our study identifies VSMC phenotypic dysregulation as a key correlate of IA instability, linking molecular deficits to clinical rupture predictors. This reframes IA as a disorder of vascular cellular identity and communication, revealing potential therapeutic targets for aneurysm stabilization.

title: CYP1B1 is a potential target of kaempferol in renal fibrosis: a multi‑omics and single‑cell transcriptomics study.
abstract: Renal fibrosis (RF) is a progressive and irreversible pathological process for which effective treatments are limited. This study explores the molecular targets and mechanisms through which kaempferol (Kae) ameliorates RF, with particular emphasis on cytochrome P450 1B1 (CYP1B1). Using a combination of transcriptomic profiling, weighted gene co‑expression network analysis (WGCNA), multi‑algorithm machine learning [least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine‑recursive feature elimination (SVM‑RFE), and Random Forest], and single‑cell transcriptomics, we identified the core targets of Kae intervention in RF. shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis evaluated gene contributions to the predictive model, while cell‑type identification by estimating relative subsets of RNA transcripts (CIBERSORT) estimated the immune microenvironment. The cell type-specific distribution of core targets was further characterized through single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and the scTenifoldKnk (a machine learning-based virtual gene knockout tool) algorithm simulated the effects of CYP1B1 loss-of-function on fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Finally, molecular docking was performed to predict the binding conformations of kaempferol with the proteins encoded by the six prioritized genes. Six core genes (VCAM1, NFKBIA, SFN, CCL5, CYP1B1, and AXL) were identified from 25 Kae-RF-related genes, with CYP1B1 as an upstream regulatory hub. Immune infiltration analysis revealed increased plasma cells and eosinophils, alongside decreased M0/M1 macrophages and activated NK cells. Single-cell analysis localized CYP1B1 to smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, with significant upregulation during late-stage fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation. Virtual knockdown of CYP1B1 upregulated 46 genes associated with fibrosis-related biological processes, including cell adhesion, G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling, ion transport, and cytoskeletal remodeling. The six-gene diagnostic model achieved area under the curves (AUCs) of 0.889 (training) and 0.759 (external validation). Molecular docking showed favorable Kae-CYP1B1 binding (- 6.5 kcal/mol). CYP1B1 may serve as a potential functional target of Kae in RF, likely through modulation of fibroblast activation and ECM remodeling. These findings are hypothesis‑generating and provide a computational basis for future experimental validation of CYP1B1‑targeted strategies in RF.

title: Multi-Omics Prioritization and Clinical Evaluation of CYP4V2 as a Candidate Biomarker in Venous Thromboembolism.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, has a substantial genetic component, but the effector genes and clinically relevant biomarkers remain incompletely defined. We analyzed FinnGen R12 genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for VTE and its subphenotypes. The Mixture model for estimating polygenicity and discoverability (MiXeR) was used to characterize the shared genetic architecture between deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Cross-tissue Unified Test for Molecular SignaTures (UTMOST) and single-tissue Functional Summary-based Imputation (FUSION) transcriptome-wide association analyses were integrated with Multi-marker Analysis of GenoMic Annotation (MAGMA) gene and pathway analyses to prioritize candidate genes. FUSION conditional and joint analysis was applied to evaluate locus-level independence. Single-variant cis-expression quantitative trait locus (cis-eQTL)-based Mendelian randomization (MR) with Steiger directionality testing was performed for CYP4V2. External validation included GSE48000 whole-blood expression analysis, Cell-type Identification By Estimating Relative Subsets Of RNA Transcripts (CIBERSORT) immune deconvolution, and serum CYP4V2 measurement by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in an independent clinical cohort. MiXeR indicated extensive shared polygenicity between deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Across UTMOST, FUSION, and MAGMA, CYP4V2 emerged as the only consensus candidate gene for VTE and its subphenotypes. FUSION conditional analysis supported locus-level prioritization. Single-variant cis-eQTL-based MR showed directionally consistent associations between genetically proxied higher CYP4V2 expression and lower risks of VTE, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism. However, regional colocalization did not support a shared CYP4V2 expression-outcome causal variant. In GSE48000, CYP4V2 expression differed between controls and study-defined recurrence-risk phenotypes and was associated with myeloid-cell composition. Serum CYP4V2 levels were lower in patients with VTE than in non-VTE controls. Integrated gene-prioritization analyses and preliminary transcriptomic and serum-protein associations nominate CYP4V2 for further evaluation as a VTE-associated candidate biomarker. Colocalization does not establish expression-mediated causality. Larger prospective studies and functional validation are required to determine its biological relevance and clinical utility.

title: An integrative meningioma surfaceome atlas and a transferable framework for CAR-T target nomination.
abstract: Meningioma is the most common primary intracranial tumor, yet recurrent and high-grade disease has few durable systemic options, and, unlike hematological malignancies, no systematically filtered cell-surface antigen resource exists to guide chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T development. We address this gap not by nominating a trial-ready target but by building two reusable resources: an integrative meningioma surfaceome atlas and a transferable, gate-based framework that separates transcriptomic discovery from CAR-T target nomination. Analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing from eight meningioma patients (GSE183655; 80,220 quality-controlled cells), patient-aware differential expression followed by a curated surfaceome filter (UniProt plasma-membrane localization; extracellular domain ≥20 aa; exclusion of ribosomal, nuclear, cytoplasmic, and secreted proteins) reduced 83 scored candidates to 13 bona fide plasma-membrane (Tier A) antigens, removing prominent false positives such as the nuclear proteins FOXC1 and MGMT, the cytoplasmic enzyme lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), and the secreted protein PTGDS.
